outline.title: Abstract
outline.description: A concise summary of the entire survey paper. It will outline the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from 2023 to 2026, covering training-time vulnerabilities (data and model poisoning), inference-time exploits (adversarial attacks and prompt injection), and output reliability issues (hallucinations). The abstract will highlight the paradigm shift from simple text-based exploits to complex vulnerabilities in autonomous agents and Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), summarizing key defense strategies and future directions.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: This section introduces the motivation and scope of the survey, detailing the rapid and sophisticated evolution of the LLM security landscape between 2023 and 2026. It will outline the transition from early prompt-based exploits and basic factual errors to deep architectural vulnerabilities, autonomous agent weaponization, and reasoning-level poisoning. The introduction will clearly define the scope of the survey, summarizing the contributions and providing a roadmap for the subsequent sections, emphasizing the critical need for robust alignment and defense mechanisms in both standard LLMs and emerging Large Reasoning Models (LRMs).

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: This section establishes the foundational concepts and terminology used throughout the survey. It will define key terms such as Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Hallucination. Furthermore, it will provide a brief overview of LLM architectures, including the recent emergence of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). Finally, it will present a comprehensive threat model overview, distinguishing between training-time threats (e.g., poisoning) and inference-time threats (e.g., adversarial attacks, prompt injection).

outline.title: 3. Data and Model Poisoning: Training-Time Vulnerabilities
outline.description: This section covers the evolution of data and model poisoning from 2023 to 2026. It will begin with early 2024 research demonstrating the fragility of RLHF and DPO, specifically how preference datasets can be manipulated via label-flipping to compromise reward models [Baumgartner_2024_RLHF, Kusaka_2025_LLM]. It will explore the expansion of poisoning into specialized domains like code generation [Yan_2024_LLM, Hossen_2024_Double] and multilingual contexts where backdoors transfer across languages [He_2024_LLMs]. Crucially, it will detail the 2025 paradigm shift toward 'behavioral' and 'reasoning' poisoning in Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), demonstrating how the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process can be hijacked to induce deceptive reasoning or force logical step-skipping [Zhu_2025_Think, Shen_2025_Decepchain].

outline.title: 4. Adversarial Attacks on LLMs
outline.description: This section details the progression of adversarial attacks from simple exploits to deep architectural vulnerabilities. It will start with foundational 2023 work on targeted data poisoning in natural language-to-code generators via 'reverse code repair' [Improta_2023_AI]. It will then cover 2024 advancements in white-box analysis tools measuring backdoor triggers in neuron activations and embeddings [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring, Nguyen_2024_Pbp]. The section will also address interaction-based vulnerabilities exploiting multi-turn conversational history [Hao_2024_Exploring] and 'context-shifting' strategies bypassing guardrails via expert programming contexts [Noever_2024_AI]. Finally, it will highlight 2025 trends focusing on autonomous agents, specifically the susceptibility of the ReAct framework to control-flow hijacking and autonomous CVE exploitation.

outline.title: 5. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: This section explores the rapid evolution of prompt injection (PI) and jailbreaking between 2024 and 2026. It will discuss early 2024 structural and formatting vulnerabilities, such as 'FlipAttack' [Liu_2024_Flipattack] and 'AutoDan' [Liu_2024_Autodan], which exploited autoregressive properties, alongside automated black-box generation frameworks using evolutionary algorithms [Zhao_2024_SQL]. The narrative will then shift to the 2025 paradigm shift toward complex, autonomous agentic systems, investigating Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in multi-modal environments like web navigation and coding editors [Shi_2025_LLM, Wang_2025_Webinject, Johnson_2025_LLM]. Furthermore, it will analyze new vulnerabilities introduced by 'Reasoning LLMs' (RLLMs) like DeepSeek-R1, specifically targeting their internal Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes [Cui_2025_LLM, Cui_2025_LLMs].

outline.title: 6. LLM Hallucinations and Factual Inconsistencies
outline.description: This section examines the transition from basic factual error detection to deep mechanistic auditing of LLM hallucinations (2024-2026). It will cover 2024 foundational work on visual hallucinations in Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), specifically the 'language prior' problem [Wang_2024_Mllm, Xing_2024_Mitigating], and the rise of Natural Language Inference (NLI) for factual consistency checking [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative]. The section will highlight 2025 advancements demonstrating that specialized small-scale models (3.8B to 8B parameters) can match or exceed GPT-4 in hallucination detection [Ivry_2025_Paladin, Yaron_2025_GPT, Paudel_2025_Hallucinot]. It will also explore the expansion into multilingual contexts [Islam_2025_LLMs, Tang_2025_Mitigating] and specialized domains such as climate science [Thulke_2025_Listen].

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: This section provides a holistic overview of defense mechanisms across the identified threat categories. It will synthesize how the field is moving from simple prompt engineering to internal activation monitoring and robust alignment techniques. Topics will include mitigating the 'language prior' in MLLMs to reduce visual hallucinations [Xing_2024_Mitigating], defending against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) in agentic workflows, and securing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes in Large Reasoning Models against behavioral poisoning. The section will evaluate the trade-offs between security guardrails, perplexity filters, and model utility.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: A MANDATORY dedicated section covering the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, tools, and evaluation frameworks utilized across all four threat categories. It will detail how Attack Success Rate (ASR) is measured for prompt injection and jailbreaks, the use of Natural Language Inference (NLI) paradigms for evaluating hallucinations [Jing_2024_Scale, Zhang_2024_Comparative], and the deployment of white-box analysis tools to measure backdoor triggers in neuron activations [Cheng_2024_Unit, Hussain_2024_Measuring]. The section will also discuss the challenges of evaluating autonomous agents and Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs), emphasizing the need for dynamic, multi-turn evaluation frameworks rather than static single-turn benchmarks.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: This section synthesizes the gaps, limitations, and future directions in LLM security research. It will discuss the ongoing arms race between automated black-box jailbreaks and dynamic defense mechanisms. A major focus will be the unresolved challenges in securing autonomous agentic systems and the inherent vulnerabilities of the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning processes in emerging RLLMs. The discussion will also highlight the difficulty of achieving robust multilingual alignment and the persistent threat of data poisoning in the model supply chain.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: The conclusion will provide a final synthesis of the survey, reiterating the critical shift from static, text-based vulnerabilities to dynamic, agentic, and reasoning-based threats. It will offer practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners, emphasizing the necessity of defense-in-depth strategies, specialized small-scale models for auditing, and the urgent need for standardized, multi-turn evaluation frameworks to ensure the safe deployment of next-generation LLMs.

background_and_preliminaries.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
background_and_preliminaries.text:
# 2. Background and Preliminaries

To establish a comprehensive foundation for understanding the security landscape of modern artificial intelligence systems, this section outlines the core concepts, methodologies, and architectures that define the current state of Large Language Models (LLMs). We begin by formalizing essential terminology, followed by an in-depth exploration of safety alignment techniques, prevailing threat models, and the emerging paradigms of Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) and Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs).

## 2.1 Terminology Definitions

Before delving into the intricacies of LLM security, it is crucial to establish a standardized vocabulary for the concepts discussed throughout this survey:

*   **Large Language Models (LLMs):** Foundation models trained on massive corpora of text data, utilizing transformer architectures to predict subsequent tokens and generate human-like text. They serve as the backbone for various downstream tasks, including translation, summarization, and code generation.
*   **LLM Agents:** Autonomous or semi-autonomous systems driven by an LLM core designed to perform specific tasks, interact with environments, or provide services based on natural language understanding [Wang_2024_LLM]. These agents often utilize tools, memory, and planning to execute complex workflows, such as website navigation or interacting with operating systems [Wang_2024_LLM].
*   **Adversarial Attacks:** Deliberate manipulations of a model's input or training data designed to induce unintended, incorrect, or malicious behavior. In the context of LLMs, this encompasses prompt injection, jailbreaking, and data poisoning.
*   **Hallucinations:** Instances where an LLM generates information that is factually incorrect, nonsensical, or ungrounded in the provided context, often presented with high confidence.
*   **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG):** A framework that enhances LLM responses by dynamically retrieving relevant information from external knowledge bases before generating an answer, thereby grounding the model's output in factual data.

## 2.2 Safety Alignment (RLHF/DPO)

As LLMs have rapidly evolved to demonstrate formidable capabilities across diverse applications, the urgency for safety and compliance has become paramount [Cheng_2024_LLM]. The core challenge of LLM safety alignment lies in the fundamental mismatch between standard pre-training objectives—which focus purely on minimizing next-token prediction errors on raw internet data—and the complex, nuanced safety requirements of human users [Cheng_2024_LLM]. To bridge this gap and reject harmful content, developers typically employ a multi-stage alignment pipeline [Chen_2024_Rmcbench].

The first stage is usually **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**, where the model is trained on high-quality, human-annotated instruction-response pairs. However, SFT alone is often insufficient for robust safety, as it heavily depends on expensive, exhaustive data collections and struggles to generalize to novel adversarial scenarios [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. 

To achieve deeper alignment, **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)** is widely utilized [Chen_2024_Rmcbench], [Liu_2025_Purpcode]. RLHF involves training a separate reward model based on human preference rankings of LLM outputs. This reward model is then used to optimize the LLM's policy via reinforcement learning algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). While effective, RLHF is notoriously complex, computationally expensive, and prone to instability during training.

Recently, **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** has emerged as a powerful alternative. Compared to the traditional RLHF framework, which relies on an explicit reward model and complex reinforcement learning loops, DPO provides a more stable and efficient end-to-end optimization path [Yu_2025_LLMs]. The core innovation of DPO is its ability to directly transform the optimization objective on a preference dataset into a maximum likelihood estimation problem for the language model itself [Yu_2025_LLMs]. By mathematically bypassing the reward model, DPO achieves comparable or superior safety alignment with significantly reduced computational overhead, making it a standard practice in modern LLM development.

## 2.3 Threat Model Overview

The deployment of LLMs in real-world applications introduces a multifaceted threat landscape. Threat models in this domain generally categorize adversaries based on their access to the model (white-box vs. black-box) and the phase of the model lifecycle they target (training vs. inference).

**Training-Time Threats:** Adversaries may attempt to compromise the model before it is even deployed. Data poisoning is a primary vector here, where malicious actors inject subtly flawed or vulnerable data into the training or fine-tuning corpora [Rubel_2024_LLM]. For example, in code-generation models, poisoned data can lead the assistant to unknowingly suggest vulnerable code to developers, effectively creating a supply chain vulnerability [Rubel_2024_LLM]. 

{{FIGURE:Tsai_2025_Beyond:attack_diagram}}

**Inference-Time Threats:** At deployment, models face a barrage of input-based attacks. Jailbreaks and prompt injections attempt to bypass the safety guardrails established during the RLHF/DPO alignment phases. Furthermore, the multi-turn interaction format of modern chat models expands the input space, allowing for a greater variety of trigger designs and backdoor insertions that are difficult to detect in single-turn evaluations [Hao_2024_Exploring]. 

The threat model is further complicated by the integration of LLMs into broader systems. In RAG systems, attackers can exploit poisoned retrieval contexts to degrade LLM efficiency, increasing output latency and energy use while preserving superficial accuracy [Wang_2025_Draincode]. Similarly, multi-agent systems inevitably interact with untrusted external inputs—such as malicious web content, files, or email attachments—creating pathways for indirect prompt injection where an adversary compromises one agent to cascade failures across the entire system [Triedman_2025_Multi].

## 2.4 Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs)

Reasoning LLMs (RLLMs) represent a paradigm shift from simple pattern matching to complex, multi-step problem solving. These models leverage techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, planning, and attribution to break down intricate tasks into manageable logical steps [Wang_2024_LLM]. This capability is essential for advanced applications like mathematical theorem proving, complex coding tasks, and autonomous agent navigation.

However, the reasoning process introduces new vulnerabilities and failure modes. LLM reasoning traces frequently suffer from complex flaws, which can be categorized into *Step Internal Flaws* (such as logical errors and localized hallucinations) and *Step-wise Flaws* (such as overthinking or underthinking a problem) [Ling_2026_Correct]. Interestingly, research indicates that simply providing correct answers during training does not consistently improve an LLM's reasoning ability; the bottleneck lies in the structure of the reasoning traces themselves rather than mere exposure to the correct final output [Ling_2026_Correct]. Adversaries can exploit these structural weaknesses by crafting inputs that force the model into infinite reasoning loops or subtly derail the logical chain, leading to confidently incorrect conclusions.

## 2.5 Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs)

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), or Vision-Language Models (VLMs), extend the capabilities of traditional text-only LLMs by integrating additional sensory modalities, most notably images, audio, and video. By projecting visual or auditory embeddings into the same latent space as text tokens, MLLMs can perform complex tasks such as visual question answering, image captioning, and multimodal reasoning.

While this integration significantly broadens the utility of foundation models, it simultaneously expands the adversarial attack surface. The continuous, high-dimensional nature of image and audio data makes it highly susceptible to imperceptible adversarial perturbations. An attacker can embed malicious instructions or jailbreak triggers directly into an image's pixels. When the MLLM processes this image, the visual encoder translates the adversarial noise into text-equivalent tokens that bypass textual safety filters, effectively hijacking the model's output. Furthermore, MLLMs are prone to multimodal hallucinations, where the model generates text that contradicts the provided visual evidence, a vulnerability that can be deliberately triggered by carefully crafted adversarial inputs. Understanding the interplay between modalities is critical for securing the next generation of AI systems.

conclusion.title: 10. Conclusion
conclusion.text:
# 10. Conclusion

The rapid proliferation of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has fundamentally transformed the landscape of artificial intelligence, bringing unprecedented capabilities alongside profound security challenges. This survey has systematically explored the multifaceted domain of adversarial attacks against these models, revealing a continuous and escalating arms race between sophisticated offensive techniques and emerging defensive paradigms. As AI systems become deeply integrated into critical infrastructure and daily workflows, understanding and mitigating these vulnerabilities is no longer optional, but an imperative for safe deployment.

**Synthesis of Trends**
Recent research underscores a distinct shift from manual, heuristic-based exploits to automated, optimization-driven adversarial attacks. Techniques such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) and automated jailbreak frameworks have demonstrated the fragility of current safety guardrails, systematically bypassing alignment protocols. Furthermore, the threat landscape has expanded beyond text-based models to encompass multimodal systems, where the intersection of vision and language introduces novel attack vectors and reasoning vulnerabilities. Concurrently, the application of LLMs in software engineering has exposed critical risks, including data poisoning in code repositories and the AI-driven synthesis of evasive malware that bypasses traditional detection engines [Rubel_2024_LLM]. The overarching macro-theme highlights an evolutionary arms race where adversaries continuously adapt to bypass static defenses.

**Defense-in-Depth**
Addressing these pervasive vulnerabilities requires moving away from monolithic safety filters toward a robust, defense-in-depth architecture. A multi-layered security posture is essential, encompassing pre-training data sanitization, robust alignment techniques during fine-tuning, and dynamic, context-aware safeguards at inference time. For instance, integrating Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks can significantly enhance the security of LLM-generated code by grounding outputs in verified security knowledge and established fixing patterns [Lin_2025_LLMs]. Such pipelines exemplify how external knowledge bases can be leveraged to intercept adversarial inputs, verify intermediate reasoning steps, and rectify potentially harmful outputs before they reach the end user.

{{FIGURE:Lin_2025_LLMs:defense_pipeline}}

**Practical Recommendations**
For practitioners and model developers, several actionable recommendations emerge from the current literature. First, comprehensive and continuous evaluation of LLM behavior across diverse, adversarial, and edge-case contexts is paramount to identifying latent weak points [Noever_2024_AI]. Developers must implement sophisticated, context-aware safeguards capable of maintaining vigilance even when conversation topics shift abruptly or when models are subjected to complex, multi-turn interactions. Additionally, organizations deploying LLM-powered coding assistants must rigorously audit training corpora to mitigate the risks of data poisoning and neural backdoors [Rubel_2024_LLM]. Implementing strict input validation and output monitoring should become standard practice in all enterprise AI deployments.

**Future Outlook**
Looking ahead, the security of foundational models will remain a critical, highly active area of research. The future outlook necessitates the development of more resilient architectures that inherently resist adversarial manipulation and reasoning hallucinations by design, rather than relying solely on post-hoc patching. As adversaries increasingly leverage AI to automate malware generation, obfuscation, and the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities, the defensive community must prioritize the creation of automated, AI-driven detection and mitigation tools [Noever_2024_AI]. Ultimately, securing the next generation of AI systems will demand collaborative efforts across academia, industry, and regulatory bodies to establish standardized, rigorous evaluation benchmarks and to foster an ecosystem where safety, transparency, and capability advance in tandem.

cross_cutting_defenses.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
cross_cutting_defenses.text:
# 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies

As the threat landscape for Large Language Models (LLMs) in software engineering expands, it has become abundantly clear that localized, single-layer defenses are insufficient. Adversaries continuously evolve their techniques, moving from explicit jailbreaks to highly sophisticated, stealthy vectors such as indirect prompt injections, latent backdoor triggers, and reasoning manipulation. Consequently, securing Code LLMs requires a defense-in-depth paradigm that cuts across the entire model lifecycle—from the processing of input contexts and the monitoring of internal latent states to the rigorous filtering of generated outputs. 

This section explores cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies that address the fundamental vulnerabilities of Code LLMs. Rather than treating the model as a black box, these strategies intervene at various stages of the generation pipeline. We examine state-of-art approaches including internal activation monitoring, the mitigation of language priors, defenses against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), the securing of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, and the deployment of robust guardrails and perplexity filters. Together, these methodologies form a comprehensive blueprint for building resilient, secure, and trustworthy AI-assisted coding systems.

## 8.1 Internal Activation Monitoring

Traditional defenses against adversarial attacks and backdoors often rely on input sanitization or output validation. However, highly optimized adversarial triggers can easily bypass these surface-level checks by blending seamlessly into benign code structures. Internal activation monitoring addresses this by shifting the defensive perimeter to the model’s latent space, observing how the neural network processes information layer by layer.

The core premise of activation monitoring is that malicious inputs—particularly backdoor triggers—force the model to traverse anomalous computational paths. When a Code LLM encounters a poisoned trigger, specific neurons or attention heads exhibit highly irregular activation spikes, effectively hijacking the model's standard generation trajectory to produce the attacker's target payload. By establishing a baseline of normal activation distributions for benign code, defenders can identify and neutralize these anomalies in real-time.

Recent advancements have formalized this approach into highly effective mitigation frameworks. For instance, the UNIT technique introduces a novel backdoor mitigation strategy designed to approximate a tight, expected distribution for each neuron during inference [Cheng_2024_Unit]. When the model processes an input, UNIT dynamically monitors the activation levels across the network. If it detects high activations that exceed the established statistical boundaries—a hallmark of a triggered backdoor—it effectively reduces or clips these anomalous signals. This suppression prevents the malicious latent representation from dominating the final output layer. Comprehensive evaluations of such techniques demonstrate high efficacy, with methods like UNIT outperforming numerous baselines across a wide array of existing attacks [Cheng_2024_Unit]. 

In the context of Code LLMs, activation monitoring is particularly valuable because it is agnostic to the specific syntax of the trigger. Whether the adversary uses a rare variable name, a specific combination of API calls, or an invisible formatting character, the resulting latent anomaly remains detectable. Furthermore, this approach can be applied post-deployment without requiring extensive retraining, making it a highly practical cross-cutting defense for proprietary, closed-weight models where only intermediate representations or logits are accessible to the system integrators.

## 8.2 Mitigating Language Priors

Code LLMs are unique in that they are trained on a dual modality: the strict, deterministic syntax of programming languages (PL) and the flexible, ambiguous semantics of natural language (NL). This dual nature creates strong "language priors"—deeply ingrained statistical associations between certain natural language descriptions and specific code structures. Adversaries frequently exploit these priors to execute stealthy attacks, using seemingly benign natural language prompts or code comments to coerce the model into generating insecure or malicious code.

Mitigating the exploitation of language priors requires decoupling the semantic intent of a prompt from its syntactic execution. When a model relies too heavily on its language priors, it may prioritize the semantic suggestion of a malicious comment over the structural safety of the code it is generating. For example, an attacker might inject a comment like `// optimize database connection for legacy support`, which exploits the model's prior association between "legacy support" and outdated, vulnerable cryptographic protocols or SQL injection-prone string concatenations.

Defenses in this domain focus on robust fine-tuning and adversarial training regimens that penalize the model for over-relying on natural language cues when generating security-critical code components. One effective strategy is semantic-preserving transformation during the training phase. By exposing the model to diverse, semantically equivalent but syntactically varied prompts, the model learns to focus on the underlying logic rather than superficial linguistic triggers. Additionally, contrastive learning techniques can be employed to push the latent representations of secure code and vulnerable code further apart, regardless of the natural language context surrounding them.

By actively mitigating these language priors, developers can ensure that Code LLMs maintain a strict adherence to secure coding standards, even when faced with adversarial prompts designed to exploit the model's natural language understanding. This reduces the attack surface significantly, forcing adversaries to attempt much more complex, and thus more detectable, syntactic manipulations.

## 8.3 Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI)

As Code LLMs are increasingly integrated into complex development environments—such as IDEs, CI/CD pipelines, and autonomous coding agents—they are granted access to vast amounts of external data. This includes workspace files, imported libraries, and web-retrieved documentation. This expanded context window introduces the critical vulnerability of Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI). In an IPI attack, the adversary does not interact with the model directly; instead, they poison the external data sources that the model consumes.

The threat of IPI is particularly severe in multi-agent systems and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) setups. As noted in recent literature, control-flow hijacking via IPI fundamentally differs from traditional jailbreaking because the user is an unwitting victim rather than the instigator [Triedman_2025_Multi]. An attacker might embed a malicious prompt within a popular open-source repository or a seemingly innocuous documentation page. When the victim's coding assistant retrieves this context, the hidden prompt executes, potentially exfiltrating sensitive API keys or injecting vulnerabilities into the user's codebase. Furthermore, attacks like DRAINCODE exploit poisoned retrieval contexts not just to alter logic, but to degrade LLM efficiency, increasing output length, latency, and energy use while preserving surface-level accuracy [Wang_2025_Draincode].

Defending against IPI requires strict compartmentalization and data provenance tracking. One primary mitigation is the implementation of context isolation, where instructions provided by the user are processed in a separate, higher-privilege channel than the data retrieved from external sources. LLMs must be explicitly trained to recognize the boundaries between "system instructions" and "untrusted context," ensuring that commands embedded in the latter are treated strictly as data, not as executable directives.

Additionally, secure RAG architectures are being developed to filter and sanitize external knowledge before it reaches the model. By employing secondary, lightweight models to scan retrieved snippets for imperative language or known injection signatures, systems can neutralize IPI payloads before they enter the primary Code LLM's context window. 

{{FIGURE:Lin_2025_LLMs:defense_pipeline}}

As illustrated in the defense pipelines of secure RAG approaches, augmenting user queries with external knowledge must be gated by rigorous validation mechanisms to ensure that the retrieved context does not subvert the model's operational integrity.

## 8.4 Securing Chain-of-Thought (CoT)

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, particularly for complex algorithmic tasks and multi-step code generation. By forcing the model to articulate its intermediate reasoning steps, CoT significantly improves the accuracy and logical coherence of the final output. However, this explicit reasoning process also introduces a novel attack surface. 

Recent studies demonstrate that while CoT models enhance code generation, they are particularly vulnerable to backdoor attacks and adversarial manipulation [Jin_2025_Guard]. Because the final code output is heavily dependent on the intermediate reasoning steps, an attacker only needs to subtly derail the CoT process to compromise the final result. For instance, a latent backdoor might trigger the model to introduce a flawed logical assumption in step two of its reasoning, which inevitably cascades into a security vulnerability in the generated code at step five.

Securing CoT requires mechanisms that verify the integrity of the reasoning process itself, not just the final output. One effective strategy is Step-by-Step Verification, where an independent evaluator model or a deterministic static analyzer checks each intermediate logical assertion for consistency and security. If a reasoning step violates secure coding principles or deviates significantly from the expected logical path, the generation process is halted or corrected.

Another approach is the use of Hidden Scratchpads. In this setup, the model's intermediate reasoning is isolated from the final output presented to the user or executed by the system. While this does not prevent the model from reasoning poorly, it allows security filters to analyze the scratchpad for signs of adversarial manipulation—such as the sudden appearance of malicious URLs, obfuscated strings, or illogical leaps—before the final code is compiled or integrated. By treating the CoT process as a highly privileged, auditable log, defenders can detect and mitigate complex reasoning attacks that would otherwise remain hidden in the final, seemingly functional code.

## 8.5 Guardrails and Perplexity Filters

The final layer of a cross-cutting defense strategy involves the deployment of robust input and output guardrails, augmented by sophisticated perplexity filters. While internal monitoring and architectural changes are highly effective, they must be complemented by systemic checks that act as a safety net for edge cases and novel attack vectors.

Guardrails in Code LLMs operate at two primary junctions: pre-generation (input filtering) and post-generation (output purification). Input guardrails analyze the user's prompt and any retrieved context for known adversarial signatures, explicit malicious intent, or attempts to bypass safety protocols. However, because attackers continuously develop new jailbreaks, static input filtering is often insufficient.

This is where Perplexity Filters become crucial. Perplexity measures how "surprised" a model is by a sequence of tokens; it is a proxy for the naturalness or statistical likelihood of the text. Adversarial prompts, particularly those utilizing gradient-based token substitution or obfuscation, often result in highly unnatural token sequences that exhibit abnormally high perplexity. Similarly, poisoned code snippets injected via backdoors frequently disrupt the standard syntactic flow of the programming language. Research indicates that it is feasible to distinguish poisoned and clean code snippets using a clean CodeLM by analyzing these token distributions, although establishing a universal threshold remains challenging due to the inherent variability of code [Sun_2025_Show].

To operationalize this, defenders employ dynamic perplexity thresholding. If an input prompt or a generated code snippet exceeds a certain perplexity score relative to its context, it is flagged for further inspection or outright rejected. For code generation, this concept is often extended to Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-aware perplexity, which evaluates the structural likelihood of the code rather than just the raw token sequence.

Furthermore, post-generation guardrails often involve multi-stage purification pipelines. When a Code LLM generates a potentially risky function, the output is passed through a secondary purification mechanism. 

{{FIGURE:Mu_2024_Codepurify:defense_pipeline}}

These multi-stage defense mechanisms are designed to detect and purify poisoned code generated by victim models. The process typically involves generating multiple masked versions of the code, analyzing the model's confidence and perplexity across these variations, and iteratively refining the output to strip away malicious payloads while preserving the intended functionality [Mu_2024_Codepurify]. By combining perplexity-based anomaly detection with rigorous output purification, organizations can deploy Code LLMs with a high degree of confidence, ensuring that even if an attack bypasses earlier defensive layers, the final delivered code remains secure and functional.

llm_hallucinations.title: 6. LLM Hallucinations and Factual Inconsistencies
llm_hallucinations.text:
**6. LLM Hallucinations and Factual Inconsistencies**

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has revolutionized natural language processing, computer vision, and human-computer interaction. Despite their unprecedented capabilities in generating fluent text, answering complex questions, and describing intricate visual scenes, these models remain fundamentally plagued by a critical vulnerability: hallucinations. Hallucinations refer to instances where a model generates content that is nonsensical, factually incorrect, or unfaithful to the provided source material or visual input. In high-stakes applications such as healthcare, legal analysis, and automated decision-making, such factual inconsistencies can have severe, real-world consequences. This section delves into the multifaceted nature of hallucinations, exploring visual hallucinations in MLLMs, the pervasive language prior problem, the application of Natural Language Inference (NLI) for ensuring factual consistency, the emergence of small-scale specialized models for efficient fact-checking, and the critical need for domain-specific grounding.

### Visual Hallucinations in MLLMs

Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) and Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have significantly expanded the frontiers of artificial intelligence by integrating visual comprehension with advanced text generation capabilities [Morbiato_2025_Grounded]. These models excel in tasks such as visual question answering (VQA), image captioning, and complex visual reasoning. However, their powerful generative capabilities are frequently undermined by visual hallucinations—a phenomenon where the model confidently describes objects, attributes, or relationships that are entirely absent from the input image [Chang_2024_Transactions].

Visual hallucinations are particularly problematic in long-form generation tasks. As the length of the generated text increases, the model's adherence to the visual input tends to degrade, leading to outputs that are partially or entirely inconsistent with the image content [Chang_2024_Transactions]. This degradation suggests a fundamental disconnect between the visual encoding process and the autoregressive language generation mechanism.

Recent empirical analyses have shed light on the underlying mechanics of these visual hallucinations. Surprisingly, research indicates that the issue may not stem from an inability to perceive the visual input. For instance, Wang et al. [Wang_2024_Mllm] demonstrated that while MLLMs may incorrectly generate non-existent objects in their final output, the models' preceding layers actually possess the capacity to accurately recognize the visual objects present in the image. This finding implies that the visual information is successfully encoded but is somehow lost, overridden, or ignored during the later stages of the generation process.

{{FIGURE:Wang_2024_Mllm:architecture_diagram}}

To mitigate these visual hallucinations, researchers have proposed various strategies. While some approaches focus on retraining or fine-tuning the models with specialized datasets, there is a growing interest in training-free mitigation methods due to their efficiency and ease of implementation. Traditional training-free methods often introduce significant inference overhead through retrospection strategies or contrastive decoding. However, novel approaches like attention reallocation (AttnReal) have been proposed to mitigate hallucinations with nearly zero extra computational cost [Tu_2025_Attention]. By dynamically adjusting the attention weights during the generation process, such methods ensure that the model remains anchored to the visual evidence, thereby reducing the likelihood of hallucinating non-existent objects.

### The Language Prior Problem

A significant driver of visual hallucinations in MLLMs is the "language prior" problem. Because MLLMs are typically built upon pre-trained Large Language Models, they inherit the strong statistical biases and linguistic priors embedded within the vast amounts of text data used during their initial training. When faced with ambiguous visual input or when generating long, complex descriptions, the model's language generation module often defaults to these learned priors rather than relying on the specific visual evidence provided.

This over-reliance on language priors manifests in several ways. For example, if an image depicts a kitchen scene, the model's language prior might strongly associate kitchens with refrigerators, stoves, and microwaves. Consequently, the model might hallucinate the presence of a microwave simply because it frequently co-occurs with other kitchen items in the textual training data, even if no microwave is visible in the actual image. The language prior effectively overrides the visual signal, leading to a hallucination.

The language prior problem is exacerbated in scenarios requiring detailed, long-form generation [Chang_2024_Transactions]. As the model generates more text, the influence of the initial visual prompt wanes, and the autoregressive nature of the language model takes over. The model becomes increasingly guided by its own generated text and its internal linguistic statistics, drifting further away from the visual ground truth. Addressing the language prior problem requires developing mechanisms that continuously reinforce the visual signal throughout the generation process, ensuring that the model's outputs remain faithful to the image rather than succumbing to statistical linguistic habits.

### NLI for Factual Consistency

Moving beyond the multimodal domain, factual consistency remains a paramount concern in text-only LLMs. A prominent approach to evaluating and enforcing factual consistency is the use of Natural Language Inference (NLI). NLI, also known as recognizing textual entailment, involves determining whether a given hypothesis (the model's output) is entailed by, contradicts, or is neutral with respect to a premise (the source text or evidence).

NLI models have been widely adopted to improve the factuality of LLM outputs across various tasks, including summarization, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and document-grounded dialogue [Harary_2025_Prefixnli]. By framing factual consistency as an entailment problem, researchers can leverage robust NLI models to automatically judge whether an LLM's generation is supported by the provided evidence.

The application of NLI for factual consistency typically involves using the NLI model as a verifier or a reward signal. At inference time, NLI can be used for beam reranking, where multiple candidate generations are produced, and the one with the highest entailment score against the source text is selected [Harary_2025_Prefixnli]. Alternatively, during the training or fine-tuning phase, NLI scores can serve as rewards in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) or similar reinforcement learning setups, explicitly training the LLM to generate entailed, factually consistent text.

This unified approach not only improves the robustness of the evaluation metrics but also provides a more comprehensive understanding of an LLM's factual reliability.

### Small-Scale Specialized Models

While using state-of-the-art, massive LLMs (such as GPT-4) as evaluators for factual consistency has become a common practice, this approach presents significant challenges. Relying on massive LLMs for fact-checking is computationally expensive, slow, and often impractical for real-time applications or large-scale processing [Tang_2024_LLMs]. Furthermore, the opacity of proprietary LLMs makes it difficult to understand their decision-making processes when evaluating factuality.

To address these limitations, there is a growing trend towards developing small-scale, specialized models dedicated specifically to factual consistency evaluation. These smaller models, often based on architectures like BERT, RoBERTa, or smaller variants of modern LLMs, are fine-tuned extensively on high-quality NLI and factuality datasets [Agarwal_2024_Zero].

The advantages of small-scale specialized models are manifold. First and foremost, they offer significantly reduced inference latency and computational costs, making them suitable for deployment in resource-constrained environments or high-throughput pipelines. Second, because they are trained specifically for the task of fact-checking, they can often achieve performance comparable to, or even exceeding, that of massive, general-purpose LLMs on specific factual consistency benchmarks.

Moreover, smaller models are generally more interpretable. Researchers can more easily analyze their attention weights, feature representations, and decision boundaries, providing valuable insights into how they assess entailment and contradiction. This transparency is crucial for building trust in automated fact-checking systems, particularly in sensitive domains. The development of these specialized models represents a crucial step towards scalable, efficient, and reliable factual consistency evaluation [Tang_2024_LLMs].

### Domain-Specific Grounding

The consequences of LLM hallucinations are most severe in high-stakes, specialized domains such as clinical medicine, law, and finance. In these fields, generating "plausible but incorrect" information can lead to misdiagnoses, flawed legal arguments, or disastrous financial decisions [Aghaebrahimian_2025_Aligncheck]. Therefore, achieving factual consistency in these areas requires more than just general-purpose NLI models; it necessitates rigorous domain-specific grounding.

Domain-specific grounding involves ensuring that an LLM's outputs are strictly anchored to verified, authoritative sources within a particular field. This is frequently achieved through Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures, where the model is provided with relevant documents retrieved from a trusted domain-specific corpus before generating its response [Tang_2024_LLMs]. However, simply providing the documents is insufficient; the model must be capable of accurately synthesizing the information without hallucinating details or drawing unsupported conclusions.

In clinical applications, for example, an LLM must accurately interpret patient records, medical literature, and clinical guidelines without introducing fabricated symptoms or treatments [Aghaebrahimian_2025_Aligncheck]. Evaluating factual consistency in this context requires specialized metrics and datasets that capture the nuances of medical terminology and clinical reasoning. General-domain NLI models often struggle with the complex, highly technical language used in these fields, highlighting the need for domain-adapted fact-checking models.

Furthermore, domain-specific grounding often requires handling complex, multi-hop reasoning across multiple documents. An LLM might need to synthesize information from a patient's history, a lab report, and a clinical guideline to formulate a correct response. Ensuring that every step of this reasoning process is factually grounded and free from hallucinations remains a significant research challenge. Future progress in this area will likely involve the development of more sophisticated RAG architectures, domain-specific pre-training strategies, and highly specialized evaluation frameworks designed to rigorously test an LLM's adherence to authoritative evidence in high-stakes environments.

### Conclusion

The challenge of hallucinations and factual inconsistencies in LLMs and MLLMs is a multifaceted problem that spans visual perception, linguistic priors, and complex reasoning. While visual hallucinations in MLLMs highlight the difficulties of aligning distinct modalities, the language prior problem underscores the powerful, sometimes detrimental, influence of pre-training data. The application of Natural Language Inference offers a robust framework for evaluating and enforcing factual consistency, and the shift towards small-scale specialized models promises more efficient and scalable fact-checking solutions. Ultimately, as LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes environments, advancing domain-specific grounding techniques will be essential to ensure that these powerful models remain reliable, trustworthy, and factually accurate tools.
